Interface PanelElement

All Known Implementing Classes:
AbstractPanelElement, Button, Checkbox, Divider, Dropdown, DropdownMulti, Flow, Icon, InfoBox, ItemDisplay, MKHudIcon, MKHudSlot, ProgressBar, Radio, ScrollContainer, Slider, TextField, TextLabel, Toggle
public interface PanelElement
A visual or interactive element within a Panel. Elements are positioned absolutely within the panel's content area (after padding) using childX/childY coordinates.

Panel elements are a decorative/interactive layer on top of the panel backgrounds. In inventory-menu panels they sit alongside slot groups (which live on the handler, not on the panel itself); in HUD panels and standalone-screen panels they are the only content.

Elements are per-panel-instance — each panel constructs its own elements via its builder. Elements aren't shared between panels.

Works uniformly across all three rendering contexts (inventory menus, HUDs, standalone screens). The RenderContext bundles per-frame state; in contexts without input dispatch (HUDs), RenderContext.hasMouseInput() returns false and mouseClicked(double, double, int) is never called by the dispatcher.

Core implementations: Button, TextLabel. Consumer mods can implement this interface for custom element types (icons, progress bars, etc.).

Coordinate contract

Two coordinate spaces are in play across the element surface:
  • Panel-local: getChildX() / getChildY() specify the element's position within the panel's content area (after padding). Fixed at construction; never mutated.
  • Screen-space: absolute coordinates in the game window's GUI-scaled pixel grid. Used by RenderContext.mouseX / RenderContext.mouseY and by the mouseX / mouseY parameters of mouseClicked(double, double, int). RenderContext.originX / RenderContext.originY are the screen-space origin of the panel's content area.
Render code composes the two: the element paints at (ctx.originX() + getChildX(), ctx.originY() + getChildY()). Input code uses screen-space directly — the dispatcher hit-tests in screen-space and passes screen-space mouseX / mouseY to mouseClicked(double, double, int). Implementations of mouseClicked(double, double, int) should trust this and not re-compose with panel-local coords.

All three dispatchers conform to this contract: the native inventory-menu dispatcher in MKCHandledScreen, the standalone-screen dispatcher in MKScreen, and the Phase 10 injection adapter ScreenPanelAdapter. Consumer implementations of PanelElement can rely on screen-space coords in mouseClicked(double, double, int) regardless of which context their panel ends up in.

    • fillWidth

      default void fillWidth(int width)
      Stretches this element to fill the given content width (the CrossAlign.FILL / column-fill primitive, Pass 3). After this call the element's getWidth() reports the filled width so panel auto-size, hit-testing, and rendering all agree — fill is NOT cosmetic.

      Default: no-op. Fixed-extent widgets (Button, labeled Toggle, Slider, Dropdown, DropdownMulti, TextField, ProgressBar, ScrollContainer, horizontal Divider) override this to set their width. Auto-content-sized widgets (TextLabel, Checkbox, Radio, ItemDisplay, Icon, and a bare/sprite Toggle switch) keep the default no-op — they remain intrinsic-width under FILL, by design: a stretched icon/switch would distort, and text reflow is owned by the panel-level screen-edge wrap, not by column fill.

      This is the deliberate capability-method answer to §0047's declined .size() hoist on AbstractPanelElement: it is not a hoisted field (per-widget storage differs), it is an optional stretch capability that each widget honors as fits its own storage.

      Parameters:
      width - the column's widest-child extent to stretch to, in pixels

    • naturalWidth

      default int naturalWidth()
      The element's NATURAL (authored / intrinsic) width before any panel width-constraint — what it wants when the panel has room. The owning Panel maxes this across its elements to compute its hug-width (contentWidth = min(maxNaturalWidth, screenEdgeCeiling)), then feeds each element a budget derived from it via layoutWithin(int).

      Distinct from getWidth(), which reports the resolved (post-constraint) width: after a narrow layoutWithin a Button's getWidth() shrinks while its naturalWidth() stays the authored value, so a later wider pass can restore it. Default returns getWidth() — correct for intrinsic-extent elements whose width never changes under constraint.

    • layoutWithin

      default void layoutWithin(int budget)
      Width flows DOWN: the owning Panel calls this every layout pass with the horizontal pixel budget available to this element (the panel's resolved content width minus this element's childX). The element resolves its presentation width — and, when it wraps a label, its height — REVERSIBLY from its immutable authored intent: a later call with a larger budget restores the natural extent (this is what fixes the historical fillWidth "ratchet", where an absolute shrink could never be undone).

      Behavioral contract by element kind:

      • Text-bearing — TextLabel, InfoBox, Button, Checkbox, Radio, a labeled Toggle, and a Dropdown's trigger label — wrap their text/label to the budget across multiple lines, growing taller to fit (and reporting the extra via extraLayoutHeight() so the panel reflows siblings below).
      • Fill widgets (Slider, TextField, ProgressBar, Divider, DropdownMulti, a Dropdown's popover rows) — cap their width to the budget so they never bleed past the panel; an over-long label scrolls/clips within bounds. These are fixed-geometry controls or live editable inputs where growing taller would distort the mechanism, so they cap rather than wrap (by design, not a gap).
      • Intrinsic widgets (Icon, ItemDisplay, a bare/sprite Toggle switch, square/sprite controls) — ignore the budget (default no-op); they keep their authored size.

      Default: no-op.

      Parameters:
      budget - horizontal pixels available to this element, in panel content space. Always >= 1.

    • extraLayoutHeight

      default int extraLayoutHeight()
      Extra vertical pixels this element occupies BEYOND its single-line / authored baseline because a label wrapped under layoutWithin(int). The owning Panel reflows the elements below a grown element downward by exactly this amount, so growth pushes — never paints over — what's beneath it (Verification-4 item 4: a panel re-stacks all its elements when one changes height). Default 0 (no growth).

    • isVisible

      default boolean isVisible()
      Returns whether this element is currently visible. Invisible elements are not rendered and don't receive clicks. Default: always visible.

      Override to gate visibility on runtime state (e.g., "show this button only when the extras panel is visible").

    • isHovered

      default boolean isHovered(RenderContext ctx)
      Returns whether the mouse is currently over this element, using the element's own bounds. Returns false in contexts without input dispatch (HUDs).

      Convenience wrapper around RenderContext.isHovered(int, int, int, int); equivalent to ctx.isHovered(getChildX(), getChildY(), getWidth(), getHeight()).

    • tooltipSupplier

      default @Nullable Supplier<net.minecraft.network.chat.Component> tooltipSupplier()
      The element's hover-tooltip text supplier, or null if none. Default null. AbstractPanelElement overrides this to return its .tooltip(...)-set field; a direct implementor (e.g. a slot) overrides it to return its own.

    • queueTooltip

      default void queueTooltip(RenderContext ctx)
      Queues this element's hover tooltip for the current frame when the cursor is over it. The per-element render(RenderContext) decides WHEN to call this (hover/suppression logic varies per widget), but the width-cap + wrap policy is centralized: it routes through MKTooltip, so every element's tooltip inherits the library-default max width automatically — never patched per call site. No-op without a tooltip, without mouse input, or when not hovered.

      Direct PanelElement implementors enable tooltips by overriding tooltipSupplier() (return their field) and calling this once at the end of render(RenderContext).

    • render

      void render(RenderContext ctx)
      Renders this element. Called during the panel background pass (screen space), after slot backgrounds.

      Position the element using the context's content origin plus this element's childX/childY: 

      int sx = ctx.originX() + getChildX();
int sy = ctx.originY() + getChildY();
      Parameters:
      ctx - per-frame render context

    • renderOverlay

      default void renderOverlay(RenderContext ctx)
      Phase 18s follow-up — second-pass render hook for ELEMENTS that draw transient overlays extending outside their layout bounds (Dropdown popovers, future tooltip-like floats, expand-on-click editors). Called by the dispatcher AFTER every element's render(RenderContext) has run, so overlays always paint on top regardless of element declaration order.

      Default: no-op. Most elements render entirely inside their layout bounds and don't need this. Override when an element has a draws-outside-bounds region that must win z-order against sibling elements (e.g., an open Dropdown's popover that should obscure a later-declared button below it).

      Sibling to getActiveOverlayBounds() — that method is the INPUT-side primitive for exclusive overlay claim; this is the RENDER-side primitive for the same conceptual overlay. An element with an active overlay typically implements both: getActiveOverlayBounds returns the overlay's bounds (input claim), renderOverlay paints it. Together they make overlays inert-on-top regardless of consumer element ordering.

      Parameters:
      ctx - per-frame render context, same instance passed to render(RenderContext) on the base pass

    • getActiveOverlayBounds

      default int @Nullable [] getActiveOverlayBounds()
      Phase 14d-5 — active overlay bounds for exclusive-claim dispatch. Called by the screen dispatchers BEFORE hitTest(double, double, int, int) as the first dispatch pass: any element returning a non-null rect from this method gets exclusive ownership of clicks (and scrolls) that fall inside the returned region. The dispatcher routes the input solely to this element regardless of mouseClicked(double, double, int)'s return value, then short-circuits — no other element (including vanilla widgets behind) sees the click.

      This is the element-level parallel to M9's panel-level modal click-eat (Panel.tracksAsModal). The use case is the same: an element that draws a transient interactive overlay outside its layout bounds (e.g., Dropdown's popover when open) needs the overlay region to be inherently inert to anything behind it. Without this primitive, a click on a popover item would also fire whichever element's layout bounds happened to overlap the popover's screen region (e.g., a button paint-occluded by the popover but still hit-testable).

      Default returns null — no active overlay. Existing elements (Button, TextField, Slider, ScrollContainer, etc.) inherit unchanged. Override only when you need a transient region that's exclusively yours.

      Coordinate space: screen-space (same as the dispatchers read mouse positions). The returned rect is consumed as [x, y, width, height].

      When to use overlay vs hitTest:

      • Overlay — the element claims an exclusive region; the region "eats" all clicks/scrolls inside it (modal-like). Use when nothing behind the region should see the input (popovers, transient action menus).
      • hitTest — the element wants to be considered for dispatch when cursor is at a non-default position; if it doesn't consume, dispatch falls through to other elements. Use when the element extends its interactive surface but isn't claiming exclusivity (extended trigger zones).
      Returns:
      [x, y, width, height] of the active overlay region, or null if no overlay is active

    • notifyClickOutsideOverlay

      default void notifyClickOutsideOverlay(double mouseX, double mouseY)
      Dismiss-side twin of getActiveOverlayBounds() — notifies an element with transient open state (a popover, an inline editor, a transient action menu) that a click landed somewhere NOT claimed by it, so it can close that state.

      The screen dispatchers call this on every visible element when a click was claimed by neither the active-overlay pass nor the hit-test pass — i.e. an "outside click." It is the element-level parallel to MKFocus.blurOnOutsideBounds(Screen, double, double), which already clears a focused TextField's focus on an outside click; this generalizes that "reset transient UI state on outside click" janitor to any popover-like element via one shared primitive (rather than each element hooking the dispatcher itself). Wired identically into every dispatcher (MKScreen, the vanilla-screen adapter, the MKC container screen) so an element behaves the same in every render context.

      Default is a no-op — elements with no transient open state inherit it unchanged. Dropdown / DropdownMulti override it to close their open popover.

      Coordinate space: screen-space, same as the dispatchers read mouse positions (the coordinates of the outside click).

      Parameters:
      mouseX - screen-space x of the click that fell outside all claims
      mouseY - screen-space y of the click that fell outside all claims

    • hitTest

      default boolean hitTest(double mouseX, double mouseY, int contentX, int contentY)
      Phase 14d-5 — interaction-bounds hit test. Called by the screen dispatchers (MKScreen, MKCHandledScreen, ScreenPanelAdapter) before mouseClicked(double, double, int) and mouseScrolled(double, double, double, double) to decide whether this element should receive the input event.

      Default implementation tests against the element's layout bounds — exactly equivalent to the inline screen-space bounds-check the dispatchers performed pre-14d-5. Existing elements (Button, TextField, Slider, ScrollContainer, etc.) inherit unchanged.

      Override for elements whose interaction surface differs from their layout bounds. Phase 14d-5's Dropdown is the canonical case: its popover renders OUTSIDE the trigger's layout bounds when open, and clicks on the popover area need to reach the Dropdown so it can route them internally (select-or-dismiss). Other future cases: tooltips with embedded action buttons, expandable inline editors, hover-with-click-targets.

      The split between layout bounds and interaction bounds is deliberate: panel auto-size logic uses getWidth / getHeight for layout, while the dispatcher uses hitTest for input routing. An element can claim a larger interaction surface (popover) without disturbing layout (which would cause panel reflow).

      Coordinate space: same as mouseClicked(double, double, int) — screen-space mouse coordinates. contentX / contentY are the panel content origin (panel position + padding); the element's screen-space top-left is contentX + getChildX(), contentY + getChildY(). The dispatcher passes its own pre-computed contentX/contentY so the element doesn't need to re-derive layout state.

      Parameters:
      mouseX - screen-space mouse X
      mouseY - screen-space mouse Y
      contentX - panel content origin X (panel.x + padding)
      contentY - panel content origin Y (panel.y + padding)
      Returns:
      true if this element wants to receive the input event

    • mouseClicked

      default boolean mouseClicked(double mouseX, double mouseY, int button)
      Called when the mouse is clicked on this element. The dispatcher hit-tests against the element's bounds before calling this method, so implementations know the click is within bounds.

      Returns true if this element consumed the click (preventing further dispatch to slots or vanilla). The default returns false, so render-only elements (TextLabel, Icon, ItemDisplay) don't need to override it.

      The button parameter is the mouse button: 0=left, 1=right, 2=middle. Core Button only consumes left-click; custom elements can handle any button.

      Parameters:
      mouseX - screen-space mouse X
      mouseY - screen-space mouse Y
      button - mouse button (0=left, 1=right, 2=middle)
      Returns:
      true if consumed, false to let the click fall through

    • mouseScrolled

      default boolean mouseScrolled(double mouseX, double mouseY, double scrollX, double scrollY)
      Called when the user scrolls the mouse wheel with the cursor over this element's bounds. The container hit-tests before calling — implementations know the cursor is within bounds.

      Returns true if this element consumed the scroll (preventing further dispatch). Default returns false, so non-scrollable elements (Button, TextLabel, etc.) don't need to override it.

      scrollX / scrollY are the wheel deltas — typically scrollY is non-zero (vertical wheel) and scrollX is zero (horizontal wheel, less common).

      Added in Phase 14d-2 alongside ScrollContainer, the first element that consumes scroll input. Existing elements default false and continue to work unchanged.

      Parameters:
      mouseX - screen-space mouse X
      mouseY - screen-space mouse Y
      scrollX - horizontal wheel delta (typically 0)
      scrollY - vertical wheel delta (positive = up, negative = down)
      Returns:
      true if consumed, false to let the scroll fall through

    • mouseReleased

      default boolean mouseReleased(double mouseX, double mouseY, int button)
      Called when the user releases a mouse button anywhere on the screen (not hit-tested against this element's bounds — the release fires regardless of cursor position, so drag-end detection works even when the user drags off the element). Default returns false for elements that don't track press/release state.

      Added in Phase 14d-2 alongside ScrollContainer to support scrollbar drag — drag is initiated in mouseClicked(double, double, int), and ends when mouseReleased fires (typically off-element since the cursor moved during drag). Existing elements default false and continue to work unchanged.

      Coordinate space: screen-space, same as mouseClicked(double, double, int).

      Parameters:
      mouseX - screen-space mouse X at release
      mouseY - screen-space mouse Y at release
      button - mouse button (0=left, 1=right, 2=middle)
      Returns:
      true if consumed (rare for release events)

    • keyPressed

      default boolean keyPressed(int keyCode, int scanCode, int modifiers)
      Keyboard input dispatch — completes the element input model alongside mouseClicked(double, double, int) / mouseScrolled(double, double, double, double). Called by the screen dispatchers on a key press while the element's panel is active. Unlike the mouse methods this is NOT hit-tested: keyboard events aren't localized to a cursor position, so every visible element on an active panel is offered the key until one consumes it.

      Returns true if this element consumed the keystroke (stopping further dispatch and suppressing vanilla's own handling of it). Default returns false, so non-keyboard elements (Button, TextLabel, …) are unaffected.

      keyCode / scanCode / modifiers are GLFW codes, matching vanilla's GuiEventListener.keyPressed. The canonical consumer is Dropdown — arrow keys move the highlighted option, Enter selects it, Escape dismisses the popover.

      Parameters:
      keyCode - GLFW key code
      scanCode - platform-specific scan code
      modifiers - GLFW modifier bitfield (shift/ctrl/alt)
      Returns:
      true if consumed, false to let the key fall through

    • isElementOpaque

      default boolean isElementOpaque()
      Returns whether this element is interaction-opaque (M9 per-element opacity). When false, clicks/hover/tooltip over this element's bounds pass through an opaque panel to the slots/screen behind it (a click-through "hole"); when true (default) the element inherits the panel's opaque click-eating behavior.

      Input-layer only — mirrors M9's panel opacity (bounding-box, not visual alpha). The panel's click-consumption (ScreenPanelRegistry) consults this before eating a click that lands on this element's bounds.

    • isInteractive

      default boolean isInteractive()
      Returns whether this element actually handles pointer input — i.e. whether a click landing on it should be treated as a solid claim that blocks the vanilla content behind it. Interactive elements (Button, TextField, Slider, Dropdown, Toggle, Checkbox, Radio, ScrollContainer) return true; render-only decorations (TextLabel, Icon, Divider, ItemDisplay, ProgressBar, InfoBox) inherit the false default.

      Why this exists (the dead-click guard). On a NON-opaque panel, the inertness contract only lets a point be claimed where a solid element sits (panelClaimsPoint branch (b)). Without this flag an opaque-but-render-only decoration would claim — and thus EAT — a click it does nothing with, contradicting the opaque(false) "clicks pass through" promise. Gating branch (b) on isElementOpaque() && isInteractive() means only elements that would actually consume the input block it; decorations stay transparent to clicks. On an OPAQUE panel the background already blocks the whole bounds, so this flag is moot there.

      Orthogonal to isElementOpaque(): opacity is "does my visual footprint occlude" (a solid Icon is opaque), interactivity is "do I consume input" (the same Icon is not interactive). Both must hold for an element to claim a point on a non-opaque panel.

      Default false — the safe direction. A custom consumer element that wants to block clicks on a transparent panel declares itself interactive; the default never produces a dead-click.

    • getElementDeclId

      default @Nullable String getElementDeclId()
      The element's explicit, stable declaration id within its panel, or null to use the default identity (its registration position in the panel's element list).

      The panel-element identity contract (THE ONE WINDOW, Address keystone). Every addressable thing needs a deterministic, reopen-stable identity so the window can resolve it by address across a screen reopen (Minecraft rebuilds the menu and all elements each open). For a panel element that identity is, by default, its registration position in the panel's immutable, consumer-built element list — the same deterministic registration-order basis a created slot uses for its localIndex. Position-as-identity is stable as long as the consumer builds the element list in the same order each open (the normal case).

      This accessor is the explicit override for when list order is not a reliable identity (e.g. a consumer who conditionally includes some elements and wants a fixed handle regardless of order): supply a stable string and the window keys on it instead of position. Mirrors the consumer-supplied-string precedent a created slot has via its panel id.

      Default null (custom consumer elements implementing this interface directly inherit position-based identity). Library elements extending AbstractPanelElement can set an explicit id via declId(String).

    • onAttach

      default void onAttach(net.minecraft.client.gui.screens.Screen screen)
      Phase 14d-3 — screen-attach lifecycle hook. Called when the containing screen reaches its init() boundary. Default no-op for elements that don't need lifecycle hooks.

      Use case: elements that wrap vanilla widgets (e.g., TextField wraps EditBox) need to register the wrapped widget via screen.addRenderableWidget(...) so vanilla's screen widget pipeline routes charTyped/keyPressed to it when focused. Without onAttach, the wrapped widget never enters vanilla's input dispatch and IME / focus / tab navigation don't work.

      v1 fires once per screen lifetime (at init); does NOT fire on panel visibility changes mid-screen-life. Visibility-driven attach/detach is deferred — see DEFERRED.md 14d-3 follow-ons.

      Coordinate space note: at onAttach time the screen has been laid out (super.init() ran before MenuKit's lifecycle hooks fire), so panel bounds + leftPos/topPos are available. Elements that register vanilla widgets typically need to update widget coords per-frame in render(RenderContext) regardless of attach-time positions.

      Parameters:
      screen - the vanilla Screen the panel is attached to

    • onDetach

      default void onDetach(net.minecraft.client.gui.screens.Screen screen)
      Phase 14d-3 — screen-detach lifecycle hook. Called when the containing screen reaches its removed() boundary. Default no-op.

      Mirrors onAttach(Screen): elements that registered vanilla widgets via screen.addRenderableWidget should remove them via screen.removeWidget(...) so vanilla's pipeline cleans up references.

      Parameters:
      screen - the vanilla Screen the panel was attached to
